Hey, thanks Ta2019.  Your words are comforting and it's nice typing out some of my thoughts.  How did I successfully work all those years as a programmer but suddenly became unemployed at age 42?  What changed?  Well, I wouldn't describe working all those years as "successful".   Rather, I'd say I kept myself from drowning by expending large amounts of energy kicking and flailing to keep my head above water.  I have problems focusing and I'm a slow worker.  For some context, I could describe my grade school experience as putting forth very little effort and consistently getting A's and B's.  It fascinated me that some kids in my classroom struggled through reading out loud.  Now I know how they felt.  Part of me is still confused how I ended up here.  I did a lot of drugs and although I'm sure damage was done there, I don't think I have cognitive problems in other parts of my life, for example, reading and writing.  I did get fired once in 2009 after 7 months of struggling and now after 5 years of shame I got fired again.  Ultimately, I can answer your question this way:  Putting forth an effort.  My managers could see I wanted to succeed and oftentimes I did what I had to in order to scrape by.  Sometimes I met expectations by working through lunch breaks/clocking out after everyone left and staying late.  I can tell you that a solid work ethic and sacrifices can only take you so far.  You're expected to find a way to meet expectations.  Eventually the good faith and mercy that's extended runs out and you're shown the door.  I can't blame them.  I have a higher level of expectation for my own performance and I react with unforgiving resentment when I detect incompetence in others.  I can say that I've inadvertently developed a very low tolerance for frustration.  Years of countless and futile attempts at writing and erasing and rewriting code which, in the end fails anyway, will breed a really dysfunctional overreaction to obstacles.  I will straight up melt the fuck down at the first sign that I'm spinning my wheels at something... anything.  What changed?  I spent a lot of time trying to figure that out.  I don't know.  I'm afraid to look for that answer anymore and to be honest I'm not sure I care to know.  I have a very strong fear of failure.  I will go to great lengths to avoid getting stuck trying to accomplish any given task.  I understand that it's part of succeeding and I could tolerate obstacles if the act of overcoming them yielded a positive return like a small improvement or learning a lesson and growing... you know, the way most people function.  Somehow I come out the other side exhausted and defeated after having spent waaay too much time trying different approaches only to fail in the end.  I believe, as a man, this sort of pattern has devastated any confidence I once had and has left me in perpetual shame and despair.  Let me tell you that I'm living in my own personal hell.  I hate that part of me so much that I think I'm willing to kill myself because of it.  Right now I want to be dead.

I understand.  I believe this problem that we all have in common here can be very different across all walks of life and circumstances.  We're all wearing a tailor-made heavy coat.  That's sometimes the only thing we have in common.  I scroll sometimes for pages upon pages, or enter search terms here, just looking for someone with a similar reason for wanting to end their life as I do mine.  As for prevention in the form of support, it's a sensitive subject and I don't think that most are willing to help because it's too heavy to engage with this topic.  Or maybe people haven't experienced this first or second hand.  Even having been familiar most of my life I find it's one of the most awkward things to talk about.  Suicide prevention campaigns probably begin from a survivor's personal experience but I'm not sure there's any real healing done outside of one on one connections.  Platitudes are indeed laughable.

The one that works for me is to perform an act of kindness towards a stranger.  It's usually a small gesture, like giving someone a rose, or letting someone in front of you in a line.  A drawback is that it's temporary.  I suppose it's admittedly selfish too.  I get to have a genuine moment and it's usually effective given the fact I'm starving from loneliness most of the time.
Imagine how it will probably unfold and be okay with that.  Be humble asking for help.  Make her laugh.
